claims.text: In FeNiCrCoCu coatings, the stable-to-unstable wear transition is driven by thermally activated dissolution of short-range order.
Increasing temperature causes a rapid decay of screw-dislocation friction in FeNiCrCoCu.
Loss of SRO-mediated resistance shifts deformation from defect-mediated plasticity to rapid lattice disorder and stacking-fault coalescence.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has a stable FCC structure at 300 K.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has high elastic modulus and stable wear resistance at 300 K.
Significant SRO strengthening is present in FeNiCrCoCu at 300 K.
A vacuum or inert atmosphere isolates mechanical and thermal effects from oxidation.
Breakdown of SRO barriers increases stacking-fault energy.
Breakdown of SRO barriers increases lattice disorder.
At room temperature, SRO creates a high barrier to dislocation motion, particularly for screw dislocations.
In MoNbTaW, the SRO strengthening effect on screw dislocations diminishes significantly at high temperature because of the entropy contribution to the free-energy barrier.
In FeNiCrCoCu, screw-dislocation critical stress decays more rapidly with temperature than edge-dislocation critical stress.
Loss of the SRO barrier permits rapid dislocation multiplication.
Loss of the SRO barrier causes stacking faults to coalesce.
FeNiCrCoCu wear resistance declines sharply at a critical temperature between 400 K and 600 K.
FeNiCrCoCu elastic modulus declines sharply between 400 K and 600 K.
The wear transition coincides with a measurable drop in screw-dislocation critical resolved shear stress.
Unstable or interrupted oxide-layer formation increases the standard deviation of the coefficient of friction.
SRO is a known strengthening mechanism specifically applicable to FCC-based high-entropy alloys.
In BCC refractory high-entropy alloys, lattice friction dominates at all temperatures.

contradictions.description: The experiment is specified to use vacuum or inert gas to isolate oxidation, yet the predicted coefficient-of-friction instability is attributed to unstable oxide-layer formation.

The mediator asserts increased stacking-fault energy, while the mechanism predicts stacking-fault coalescence without explaining how fault structures proliferate despite the increased energetic cost of forming them.

The mechanism relies on temperature-induced decay of screw-dislocation friction in the BCC refractory MoNbTaW system, whereas the boundary states that lattice friction dominates BCC refractory alloys at all temperatures.
